title: Ὀδυσσεὺς πτωχεύων ἐν μεγάροις
titleEn: Odysseus Begs in the Hall — Odyssey 17.306–408
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Still disguised as a beggar, Odysseus sees the old dog Argus lying in the dung and asks Eumaeus about him. Eumaeus describes what the dog once was, says his master died far away, and goes in to the suitors; Argus, who has seen Odysseus after twenty years, dies at that moment. Telemachus beckons the swineherd to a stool beside his table. Odysseus comes in behind him and sits on the threshold, and Telemachus sends him bread and meat with the message that he may beg from all the suitors. Odysseus prays for Telemachus and eats. When the singer stops, Athena urges him to go round the suitors, begging and learning which of them are lawless. Melanthius says he has seen the stranger before, Antinous abuses Eumaeus for bringing him, and Eumaeus answers sharply. Telemachus bids Eumaeus be silent and tells Antinous to give the stranger something; Antinous replies with a jibe, and his speech goes on into the next part.

sentences.t: Εὔμαι’, ἦ μάλα θαῦμα, κύων ὅδε κεῖτ’ ἐνὶ κόπρῳ.
sentences.tr: Eumai’, ē mala thauma, kyōn hode keit’ eni koprōi.
sentences.l: “Eumaeus, truly a marvel: this dog lies in the dung.
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, what a marvel: this dog is lying in the dung.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks, as a stranger who has just seen the dog. Εὔμαι’ is the vocative of Εὔμαιος with its last vowel elided. ἦ μάλα θαῦμα is ‘truly a marvel’, with no verb. κεῖτ’ is κεῖται, elided, and the present tense matters: he sees the dog as he speaks, where the poet’s κεῖτ’ at 296 and 300 was κεῖτο ‘lay’. κόπρῳ is ‘in the dung’, the heap of 297.

sentences.t:
καλὸς μὲν δέμας ἐστίν, ἀτὰρ τόδε γ’ οὐ σάφα οἶδα,
εἰ δὴ καὶ ταχὺς ἔσκε θέειν ἐπὶ εἴδεϊ τῷδε,
ἦ αὔτως οἷοί τε τραπεζῆες κύνες ἀνδρῶν
γίγνοντ’·
sentences.tr:
kalos men demas estin, atar tode g’ ou sapha oida,
ei dē kai tachys eske theein epi eideï tōide,
ē autōs hoioi te trapezēes kynes andrōn
gignont’·
sentences.l:
Fair in body he is, but this I do not clearly know,
whether indeed he was also swift to run, along with this form,
or merely such as table-dogs, dogs of men,
become;
sentences.i: He is fair in body, but this I do not clearly know: whether he was also swift at running, to match this appearance, or whether he is merely like the dogs that men keep at their tables;
sentences.n: καλὸς … δέμας is ‘fair in body’, δέμας being an accusative of respect. The question runs from εἰ δή ‘whether’: ἔσκε is an iterative past of εἰμί, ‘was (as a rule)’, with θέειν ‘to run’ (uncontracted θεῖν), and ἐπὶ εἴδεϊ τῷδε is ‘in addition to this form’. ἦ means ‘or’ here. τραπεζῆες κύνες is ‘table dogs’, from τράπεζα ‘table’; αὔτως ‘merely’; γίγνοντ’ is γίγνονται, ‘come to be’.

sentences.t: ἀγλαΐης δ’ ἕνεκεν κομέουσιν ἄνακτες.
sentences.tr: aglaïēs d’ heneken komeousin anaktes.
sentences.l: and for the sake of splendour lords tend them.”
sentences.i: and their lords tend them for the sake of splendour.”
sentences.n: The cut falls mid-line, after the stop that ends the question. ἀγλαΐης is the genitive of ἀγλαΐη ‘splendour, show’, the singular of the word at 17.244, and ἕνεκεν ‘for the sake of’ governs it. κομέουσιν is κομέω ‘tend, take care of’, uncontracted (Attic κομοῦσιν). ἄνακτες ‘lords’ are the dogs’ masters. Odysseus knows the answer and asks as a stranger would.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply, with the poet’s turn to speak to Eumaeus as ‘you’: προσέφης is the second person where the formula usually has the third, προσέφη. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα, ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’, is a vocative. The same line recurs at 380.

sentences.t: καὶ λίην ἀνδρός γε κύων ὅδε τῆλε θανόντος.
sentences.tr: kai liēn andros ge kyōn hode tēle thanontos.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, this dog is a man’s who died far away.
sentences.i: “Yes, indeed, this is the dog of a man who died far away.
sentences.n: Eumaeus answers without knowing who stands before him. καὶ λίην is ‘yes, quite so’, and the genitive ἀνδρὸς … θανόντος, ‘of a man who has died’, says whose dog it is; τῆλε is ‘far away’. The words are heavy with irony: the dead man is the stranger himself. ὅδε ‘this’ points at the dog, and γε gives the reply its emphasis.

sentences.t:
εἰ τοιόσδ’ εἴη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργα,
οἷόν μιν Τροίηνδε κιὼν κατέλειπεν Ὀδυσσεύς,
αἶψά κε θηήσαιο ἰδὼν ταχυτῆτα καὶ ἀλκήν.
sentences.tr:
ei toiosd’ eiē ēmen demas ēde kai erga,
hoion min Troiēnde kiōn kateleipen Odysseus,
aipsa ke thēēsaio idōn tachytēta kai alkēn.
sentences.l:
If such he were, both in body and in deeds,
as him, to Troy going, left Odysseus,
quickly you would marvel, seeing his speed and might.
sentences.i: If he were still such, in body and in performance, as Odysseus left him when he went to Troy, you would quickly marvel to see his speed and might.
sentences.n: A condition with the optative: εἰ … εἴη ‘if he were’, answered by κε with the optative θηήσαιο ‘you would marvel at’ (θηέομαι, with a long η in Homer). τοιόσδε … οἷον is ‘such … as’. κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’, and Τροίηνδε has the suffix -δε ‘to Troy’. ἔργα is ‘deeds’, what the dog could do. ταχυτῆτα is ‘speed’, ἀλκήν ‘might’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι φύγεσκε βαθείης βένθεσιν ὕλης
κνώδαλον, ὅττι δίοιτο·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar ti phygeske batheiēs benthesin hylēs
knōdalon, hotti dioito·
sentences.l:
For not at all would it escape, in the depths of deep forest,
a wild beast, whatever he chased;
sentences.i: For no wild beast that he chased would ever escape him in the depths of the deep forest;
sentences.n: φύγεσκε has the iterative suffix -σκ-, as ἀγίνεσκον at 294: a thing that happened every time, ‘would escape’. κνώδαλον is ‘wild beast’, the subject, held back to the second line. βένθεσιν is a dative of place, ‘in the depths’ (βένθος = βάθος), with βαθείης ὕλης ‘deep forest’. ὅττι is ὅ τι ‘whatever’, and δίοιτο is the optative of δίεμαι ‘chase’, the optative of a general condition in the past.

sentences.t: καὶ ἴχνεσι γὰρ περιῄδη·
sentences.tr: kai ichnesi gar periēidē·
sentences.l: for in tracks too he was exceedingly skilled;
sentences.i: for he was also unusually good at following a track;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason the dog never lost a beast. καί is ‘also’. ἴχνεσι is the dative of ἴχνος ‘track, footprint’, and περιῄδη is the pluperfect of περιοίδα ‘know beyond others, be exceptionally skilled’, with the old ending -η for -ει (Attic ᾔδειν). The dative says what he was skilled in: ‘in tracks’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἔχεται κακότητι, ἄναξ δέ οἱ ἄλλοθι πάτρης
ὤλετο, τὸν δὲ γυναῖκες ἀκηδέες οὐ κομέουσι.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ echetai kakotēti, anax de hoi allothi patrēs
ōleto, ton de gynaikes akēdees ou komeousi.
sentences.l:
but now he is held by misery, and his lord elsewhere than his fatherland
perished, and him the women, uncaring, do not tend.
sentences.i: But now he is in the grip of misery; his lord has perished far from his fatherland, and the women, caring nothing for him, do not tend him.
sentences.n: ἔχεται is the middle of ἔχω, ‘is held’, with κακότητι ‘by misery’ as a dative of the means. ἄλλοθι πάτρης is ‘elsewhere than his fatherland’, ἄλλοθι taking the genitive. ὤλετο is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, ‘perished’, and keeps its augment (the unaugmented form is ὄλετο). γυναῖκες are the women of the house, here the servants. ἀκηδέες is ‘uncaring’, built on κῆδος ‘care’ with the negative ἀ-. κομέουσι is ‘tend’, as at 310.

sentences.t:
δμῶες δ’, εὖτ’ ἂν μηκέτ’ ἐπικρατέωσιν ἄνακτες,
οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐθέλουσιν ἐναίσιμα ἐργάζεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
dmōes d’, eut’ an mēket’ epikrateōsin anaktes,
ouket’ epeit’ ethelousin enaisima ergazesthai·
sentences.l:
And servants, when no longer hold sway the lords,
no longer then are willing to do what is fitting;
sentences.i: Servants, once their lords no longer hold sway over them, are no longer willing to do what is fitting;
sentences.n: A general saying. δμῶες are ‘servants’, with the subordinate clause εὖτ’ ἂν … ἐπικρατέωσιν ‘when … hold sway’, a subjunctive in an uncontracted form (Attic ἐπικρατῶσιν). μηκέτι and οὐκέτι both mean ‘no longer’, and the second repeats the first. ἐναίσιμα is ‘what is fitting’, from αἶσα ‘portion’, and ἐργάζεσθαι is ‘to work, to do’.

sentences.t:
ἥμισυ γάρ τ’ ἀρετῆς ἀποαίνυται εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἀνέρος, εὖτ’ ἄν μιν κατὰ δούλιον ἦμαρ ἕλῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
hēmisy gar t’ aretēs apoainytai euryopa Zeus
aneros, eut’ an min kata doulion ēmar helēisin.
sentences.l:
For half of excellence takes away far-thundering Zeus
of a man, when him the day of slavery seizes.”
sentences.i: For Zeus who thunders from afar takes away half of a man’s excellence, once the day of slavery takes hold of him.”
sentences.n: ἥμισυ is ‘half’, and ἀρετῆς … ἀνέρος, ‘of a man’s excellence’, is the genitive of what is halved. ἀποαίνυται is ἀπαίνυται ‘takes away’, and τε marks a general truth. εὖτ’ ἄν is ‘when’, with the subjunctive ἕλῃσιν; κατά is separated from it by tmesis, ‘seizes’. δούλιον ἦμαρ is ‘the day of slavery’ (see 14.340). εὐρύοπα Ζεύς, ‘Zeus who thunders from afar’, is the standing name-phrase; the second element is disputed (ὄψ ‘voice’ or ‘eye, face’), and the traditional gloss ‘thundering’ is followed.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν εἰσῆλθε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
βῆ δ’ ἰθὺς μεγάροιο μετὰ μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn eisēlthe domous eu naietaontas,
bē d’ ithys megaroio meta mnēstēras agauous.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he entered the well-inhabited house,
and went straight through the hall to the noble suitors.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went into the well-inhabited house, and straight through the hall to the noble suitors.
sentences.n: Eumaeus is the subject, and ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes his speech. The plural δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας is the formula for one dwelling, ‘the well-inhabited house’. βῆ δ’ ἰθύς is ‘went straight’, and μεγάροιο is a genitive of the way, ‘through the hall’. μετά with the accusative gives the goal, ‘to’. μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς is ‘the noble suitors’, a standing phrase.

sentences.t:
Ἄργον δ’ αὖ κατὰ μοῖρ’ ἔλαβεν μέλανος θανάτοιο,
αὐτίκ’ ἰδόντ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἐεικοστῷ ἐνιαυτῷ.
sentences.tr:
Argon d’ au kata moir’ elaben melanos thanatoio,
autik’ idont’ Odysēa eeikostōi eniautōi.
sentences.l:
And Argus in turn the fate seized of black death,
at once having seen Odysseus in the twentieth year.
sentences.i: And Argus, at the very moment he saw Odysseus in the twentieth year, was seized by the fate of black death.
sentences.n: The subject is μοῖρα ‘fate’, and Ἄργον is its object; κατά … ἔλαβεν is tmesis for κατέλαβεν ‘seized’. μέλανος θανάτοιο is ‘of black death’. ἰδόντ’ is ἰδόντα, the aorist participle agreeing with Ἄργον: he is the one who saw. αὐτίκα is ‘at once’. ἐεικοστῷ ἐνιαυτῷ is ‘in the twentieth year’, a dative of time, counting from Odysseus’s departure.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πολὺ πρῶτος ἴδε Τηλέμαχος θεοειδὴς
ἐρχόμενον κατὰ δῶμα συβώτην, ὦκα δ’ ἔπειτα
νεῦσ’ ἐπὶ οἷ καλέσας·
sentences.tr:
ton de poly prōtos ide Tēlemachos theoeidēs
erchomenon kata dōma sybōtēn, ōka d’ epeita
neus’ epi hoi kalesas·
sentences.i: Telemachus, godlike in form, was by far the first to see the swineherd as he came through the house, and he quickly nodded to him, calling him to his side;
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, taken up by συβώτην in the next line, so that ‘him … the swineherd’ is the object of ἴδε (unaugmented). πολὺ πρῶτος is ‘by far the first’. ἐρχόμενον κατὰ δῶμα is ‘coming through the house’. νεῦσ’ is νεῦσε, elided and unaugmented (Attic ἔνευσε), ‘nodded’, and ἐπὶ οἷ καλέσας is ‘calling him to himself’, οἷ being ‘to him’; the same words recur at 342. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ παπτήνας ἕλε δίφρον
κείμενον, ἔνθα τε δαιτρὸς ἐφίζεσκε κρέα πολλὰ
δαιόμενος μνηστῆρσι δόμον κάτα δαινυμένοισι·
sentences.tr:
ho de paptēnas hele diphron
keimenon, entha te daitros ephizeske krea polla
daiomenos mnēstērsi domon kata dainymenoisi·
sentences.i: and Eumaeus looked about and took a stool that lay where the carver used to sit, dividing up much meat for the suitors as they feasted throughout the house;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is the swineherd, and παπτήνας is the aorist participle of παπταίνω ‘look about’. δίφρος is a seat without a back, ‘stool’; the word means ‘chariot’ elsewhere. κείμενον agrees with it. ἐφίζεσκε has the iterative suffix, ‘used to sit’, and δαιόμενος is the middle participle of δαίω ‘divide’; δαιτρός is the ‘carver’. δόμον κάτα is κατὰ δόμον with the preposition after its noun, ‘throughout the house’, and δαινυμένοισι is ‘feasting’.

sentences.t:
τὸν κατέθηκε φέρων πρὸς Τηλεμάχοιο τράπεζαν
ἀντίον, ἔνθα δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτὸς ἐφέζετο·
sentences.tr:
ton katethēke pherōn pros Tēlemachoio trapezan
antion, entha d’ ar’ autos ephezeto·
sentences.l:
this he put down, carrying it, by Telemachus’ table
opposite, and there he himself sat down;
sentences.i: He carried it over and set it down opposite, by Telemachus’ table, and there he sat down himself;
sentences.n: τόν is the stool, the object of κατέθηκε ‘set down’ with φέρων ‘carrying’. πρὸς … τράπεζαν is ‘towards the table’, the genitive Τηλεμάχοιο ending in -οιο (Attic -ου). ἀντίον is ‘opposite’, facing Telemachus, and ἔνθα ‘there’ refers back to the same spot. ἐφέζετο is the imperfect middle of ἐφέζομαι ‘sit down’, and αὐτός stresses that it is Eumaeus who sits.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρα κῆρυξ
μοῖραν ἑλὼν ἐτίθει κανέου τ’ ἐκ σῖτον ἀείρας.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ara kēryx
moiran helōn etithei kaneou t’ ek siton aeiras.
sentences.l:
and for him a herald a portion having taken was setting,
and from the basket bread lifting.
sentences.i: and a herald took a portion and set it before him, lifting bread from the basket.
sentences.n: τῷ is a dative pronoun, ‘for him’, Eumaeus. μοῖραν is ‘a portion’, and ἐτίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι, ‘was setting’. σῖτον is ‘bread’, as in the earlier banquets, and κανέου is a genitive of κάνεον ‘basket’ with ἐκ, the preposition standing after τ’. ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δὲ μετ’ αὐτὸν ἐδύσετο δώματ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἐναλίγκιος ἠδὲ γέροντι,
σκηπτόμενος·
sentences.tr:
anchimolon de met’ auton edyseto dōmat’ Odysseus,
ptōchōi leugaleōi enalinkios ēde geronti,
skēptomenos·
sentences.i: Close behind him Odysseus came into the house, looking like a pitiful beggar, an old man, propping himself on a staff;
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is ‘close by, close behind’, and μετ’ αὐτόν ‘after him’ is Eumaeus. ἐδύσετο is the aorist of δύομαι, ‘entered’. ἐναλίγκιος is ‘like’ with the dative: πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ‘a pitiful beggar’, joined by ἠδέ to γέροντι ‘an old man’. σκηπτόμενος is a middle participle of σκήπτω, ‘propping himself’; the staff is understood, not named. The stop after it is an ano teleia.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ λυγρὰ περὶ χροΐ εἵματα ἕστο.
sentences.tr: ta de lygra peri chroï heimata hesto.
sentences.l: and the grievous clothes about his skin he wore.
sentences.i: and he wore grievous clothes about his body.
sentences.n: The cut falls mid-line. τά is a pronoun used like an article, ‘those’, with λυγρὰ … εἵματα ‘grievous clothes’ (the beggar’s rags, as at 16.457). χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’, and ἕστο is the pluperfect passive of ἕννυμι, ‘was clothed in’, so that the clothes are ‘worn about his body’.

sentences.t:
ἷζε δ’ ἐπὶ μελίνου οὐδοῦ ἔντοσθε θυράων,
κλινάμενος σταθμῷ κυπαρισσίνῳ, ὅν ποτε τέκτων
ξέσσεν ἐπισταμένως καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν.
sentences.tr:
hize d’ epi melinou oudou entosthe thyraōn,
klinamenos stathmōi kyparissinōi, hon pote tektōn
xessen epistamenōs kai epi stathmēn ithynen.
sentences.l:
And he sat on an ashen threshold inside the doors,
leaning on a cypress post, which once a carpenter
planed skilfully and straightened to the line.
sentences.i: He sat down on the ashwood threshold just inside the doors, leaning against a cypress post that a carpenter had once planed skilfully and trued straight to the line.
sentences.n: ἷζε is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit down’. μελίνου is ‘of ash-wood’ (μελίη ‘ash’), with οὐδοῦ ‘threshold’, and ἔντοσθε θυράων ‘inside the doors’. κλινάμενος is the aorist middle participle of κλίνω ‘lean’, and σταθμῷ is the dative of σταθμός ‘post’. ὅν ‘which’ is the relative. The last line is the same as 5.244 except that 5.244 has ξέσσε δ’ where this has ξέσσεν: ‘planed skilfully’ and ‘straightened to the line’ (στάθμη ‘carpenter’s line’).

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἐπὶ οἷ καλέσας προσέειπε συβώτην,
ἄρτον τ’ οὖλον ἑλὼν περικαλλέος ἐκ κανέοιο
καὶ κρέας, ὥς οἱ χεῖρες ἐχάνδανον ἀμφιβαλόντι·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’ epi hoi kalesas proseeipe sybōtēn,
arton t’ oulon helōn perikalleos ek kaneoio
kai kreas, hōs hoi cheires echandanon amphibalonti·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus, calling the swineherd to himself, addressed him,
a loaf, whole, taking from the very fair basket
and meat, as much as his hands could hold, to him having thrown them round it:
sentences.i: And Telemachus called the swineherd to him and spoke to him, taking a whole loaf from the very fair basket, and meat, as much as his two hands could hold when he closed them round it:
sentences.n: καλέσας ‘calling’ is the same phrase as at 330. ἄρτον is ‘loaf’ and οὖλον ‘whole’, the traditional sense of the word here; ἑλών ‘taking’ governs ἄρτον and κρέας. περικαλλής ‘very fair’ goes with κανέοιο, a genitive in -οιο. ὥς οἱ χεῖρες ἐχάνδανον is ‘as much as his hands could hold’, ἐχάνδανον being an imperfect of χανδάνω; ἀμφιβαλόντι is dative, agreeing with οἱ: ‘for him, having thrown them round it’.

sentences.t:
δὸς τῷ ξείνῳ ταῦτα φέρων αὐτόν τε κέλευε
αἰτίζειν μάλα πάντας ἐποιχόμενον μνηστῆρας·
sentences.tr:
dos tōi xeinōi tauta pherōn auton te keleue
aitizein mala pantas epoichomenon mnēstēras·
sentences.l:
“Give to the stranger these things, carrying them, and him himself bid
to beg, going round to every one of them, the suitors;
sentences.i: “Take this and give it to the stranger, and tell him to go round all the suitors and beg of them, every one;
sentences.n: Telemachus speaks to Eumaeus. δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and τῷ ξείνῳ is ‘to the stranger’, the first word a pronoun used like an article. ταῦτα is ‘these things’, the loaf and meat. αὐτόν is ‘him himself’, the object of κέλευε ‘bid’, with the infinitive αἰτίζειν ‘to beg’. μάλα πάντας is ‘every one’, and ἐποιχόμενον is ‘going round’, agreeing with αὐτόν. μνηστῆρας is the object of αἰτίζειν. Its second line, 346, recurs at 351.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς δ’ οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι.
sentences.tr: aidōs d’ ouk agathē kechrēmenōi andri pareinai.
sentences.l: and shame is not good to be present for a needy man.”
sentences.i: since shame is no good companion to a man in need.”
sentences.n: αἰδώς is ‘shame’, the reluctance that holds a man back, here from asking. The verb is left out, so the line reads ‘shame is not good to be present for a needy man’: παρεῖναι is an infinitive of purpose or respect, ‘to be there’, and κεχρημένῳ is a perfect participle in the dative, ‘in need’. δέ gives the reason for the order just given.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, βῆ δὲ συφορβός, ἐπεὶ τὸν μῦθον ἄκουσεν,
ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευε·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, bē de syphorbos, epei ton mython akousen,
anchou d’ histamenos epea pteroent’ agoreue·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and went the swineherd, when the word he heard,
and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the swineherd, when he had heard the word, went and stood close beside him and spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο closes Telemachus’s speech, and βῆ δέ ‘he went’ is the swineherd, here συφορβός, a by-form of ὑφορβός (συς ‘swine’ and φέρβω ‘feed’). τὸν μῦθον is ‘the word’, τόν a pronoun used like an article. ἀγχοῦ ἱστάμενος is ‘standing close by’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the formula ‘winged words’, and ἀγόρευε ‘spoke’ is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχός τοι, ξεῖνε, διδοῖ τάδε, καί σε κελεύει
αἰτίζειν μάλα πάντας ἐποιχόμενον μνηστῆρας·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos toi, xeine, didoi tade, kai se keleuei
aitizein mala pantas epoichomenon mnēstēras·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus gives you these things, stranger, and bids you
to beg, going round to every one of them, the suitors;
sentences.i: “Telemachus gives you this, stranger, and bids you go round all the suitors and beg of them, every one;
sentences.n: Eumaeus repeats the message, and its second line is the same as 346. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and διδοῖ is the epic third person of δίδωμι (Attic δίδωσι). τάδε ‘these things’ points ahead to what he holds out. καί σε κελεύει is ‘and bids you’, with the same infinitive αἰτίζειν as before, so ‘you’ now takes the place of ‘him’.

sentences.t: αἰδῶ δ’ οὐκ ἀγαθήν φησ’ ἔμμεναι ἀνδρὶ προΐκτῃ.
sentences.tr: aidō d’ ouk agathēn phēs’ emmenai andri proïktēi.
sentences.l: and shame, he says, is not good for a man, a beggar.”
sentences.i: and he says that shame is no good to a beggar.”
sentences.n: φησ’ is φησί ‘he says’, with the infinitive ἔμμεναι (Attic εἶναι) ‘to be’ and the accusative αἰδῶ … οὐκ ἀγαθήν ‘shame … not good’. αἰδῶ is the accusative of αἰδώς. ἀνδρὶ προΐκτῃ is ‘for a man, a beggar’, προΐκτης being a rarer word for ‘beggar’, a dative here. The thought is Telemachus’s at 347, slightly shortened.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply. τόν is ‘him’, Eumaeus, and ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’, and πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is a standing epithet of Odysseus (μῆτις ‘cunning’).

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ ἄνα, Τηλέμαχόν μοι ἐν ἀνδράσιν ὄλβιον εἶναι,
καί οἱ πάντα γένοιθ’ ὅσσα φρεσὶν ᾗσι μενοινᾷ.
sentences.tr:
Zeu ana, Tēlemachon moi en andrasin olbion einai,
kai hoi panta genoith’ hossa phresin hēisi menoināi.
sentences.l:
“Zeus, lord, Telemachus for me among men prosperous to be,
and for him all things may come to be, as many as in his own mind he intends.”
sentences.i: “Lord Zeus, I pray that Telemachus may be prosperous among men, and that everything he has in mind may come to him.”
sentences.n: Odysseus answers with a prayer for Telemachus. Ζεῦ ἄνα is ‘lord Zeus’ (ἄνα a vocative of ἄναξ), and the infinitive εἶναι stands for a wish, ‘may he be’, with μοι ‘for me’. ὄλβιον is ‘prosperous’, as the same word is rendered elsewhere. γένοιθ’ is γένοιτο, an optative of wish, and ὅσσα is ‘as many as’. ᾗσι is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and μενοινᾷ is ‘intends’, a form of μενοινάω.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφοτέρῃσιν ἐδέξατο καὶ κατέθηκεν
αὖθι ποδῶν προπάροιθεν, ἀεικελίης ἐπὶ πήρης,
ἤσθιε δ’ ἧος ἀοιδὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἄειδεν·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai amphoterēisin edexato kai katethēken
authi podōn proparoithen, aeikeliēs epi pērēs,
ēsthie d’ hēos aoidos eni megaroisin aeiden·
sentences.i: So he said, and received it with both hands and set it down right there in front of his feet, on his unseemly wallet, and ate while the minstrel sang in the halls;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is the formula ‘so he spoke, and’, which closes a speech and moves the story on. ἐδέξατο is the aorist middle of δέχομαι ‘receive’, and ἀμφοτέρῃσιν is ‘with both’, the word ‘hands’ being understood. αὖθι is ‘right there’, and ποδῶν προπάροιθεν ‘before his feet’. ἀεικελίης is ‘unseemly’, an epic form of ἀεικής, with πήρης ‘wallet’. ἧος is ‘while’ and ἄειδεν ‘was singing’, uncontracted.

sentences.t: εὖθ’ ὁ δεδειπνήκειν, ὁ δ’ ἐπαύετο θεῖος ἀοιδός.
sentences.tr: euth’ ho dedeipnēkein, ho d’ epaueto theios aoidos.
sentences.l: when he had eaten his meal, and he was ceasing, the divine minstrel.
sentences.i: and just as he had eaten his meal, the divine minstrel stopped.
sentences.n: εὖθ’ is the epic form of εὖτε ‘when’. The two ὁ are pronouns for two different men: the first is Odysseus, who ‘had eaten his meal’ (δεδειπνήκειν, a pluperfect without augment, with movable ν), the second the singer. ἐπαύετο is the imperfect middle of παύω, ‘was ceasing’. θεῖος ἀοιδός is ‘divine minstrel’, the standing phrase. The line ends in a full stop.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δ’ ὁμάδησαν ἀνὰ μέγαρ’.
sentences.tr: mnēstēres d’ homadēsan ana megar’.
sentences.l: And the suitors made an uproar throughout the hall.
sentences.i: The suitors broke into uproar throughout the hall.
sentences.n: ὁμάδησαν is the aorist of ὁμαδέω ‘make a din’. ἀνὰ μέγαρ’ is ἀνὰ μέγαρα, ‘up and down the hall’, with the final vowel elided. The unit ends mid-line, at the stop after μέγαρ’, and the next sentence opens with αὐτάρ.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη,
ἄγχι παρισταμένη Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα
ὤτρυν’, ὡς ἂν πύρνα κατὰ μνηστῆρας ἀγείροι,
γνοίη θ’ οἵ τινές εἰσιν ἐναίσιμοι οἵ τ’ ἀθέμιστοι·
sentences.tr:
autar Athēnē,
anchi paristamenē Laertiadēn Odysēa
ōtryn’, hōs an pyrna kata mnēstēras ageiroi,
gnoiē th’ hoi tines eisin enaisimoi hoi t’ athemistoi·
sentences.l:
But Athena,
close by, standing near, the son of Laertes, Odysseus,
urged on, that wheaten loaves among the suitors he might gather,
and might learn who are those with a sense of what is fitting and who the lawless;
sentences.i: But Athena, standing close beside Odysseus, son of Laertes, urged him on to gather wheaten loaves among the suitors and to learn which of them had a sense of what is fitting and which were lawless;
sentences.n: The subject Ἀθήνη stands at the end of 360 and is described by παρισταμένη ‘standing near’, ἄγχι ‘close by’; Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα, ‘Odysseus, son of Laertes’, is the object of ὤτρυν’ ‘urged on’. ὡς ἂν with the optative gives purpose: ἀγείροι ‘he might gather’ and γνοίη ‘he might learn’. πύρνα is ‘wheaten loaves’. ἐναίσιμοι is ‘having a sense of what is fitting’ and ἀθέμιστοι ‘lawless’, from θέμις.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς τιν’ ἔμελλ’ ἀπαλεξήσειν κακότητος.
sentences.tr: all’ oud’ hōs tin’ emell’ apalexēsein kakotētos.
sentences.l: But not even so was she going to ward off from misery any of them.
sentences.i: But even so she was not going to keep any of them from misery.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘not even so’, ὥς being the adverb. ἔμελλε with the future infinitive ἀπαλεξήσειν is ‘was going to’, and the verb takes a genitive of what is warded off, κακότητος ‘from misery’; τιν’ is ‘anyone’, one of the suitors. The subject is not named, and Athena of 360–361 is the likelier one, though Odysseus could be meant; the translation takes Athena. Either way the sentence tells the audience that the test will not save anyone.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν αἰτήσων ἐνδέξια φῶτα ἕκαστον,
πάντοσε χεῖρ’ ὀρέγων, ὡς εἰ πτωχὸς πάλαι εἴη.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ imen aitēsōn endexia phōta hekaston,
pantose cheir’ oregōn, hōs ei ptōchos palai eiē.
sentences.l:
He set out to go to beg, towards the right, each man,
in every direction his hand stretching out, as if a beggar he had long been.
sentences.i: He set out to beg of each man in turn, going round to the right and holding out his hand on every side, as if he had long been a beggar.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is ‘he set out to go’, and αἰτήσων is a future participle of purpose, ‘to beg’, with φῶτα ἕκαστον ‘each man’. ἐνδέξια is ‘towards the right’, the direction in which a company is served. πάντοσε is ‘in every direction’, and ὀρέγων is ‘stretching out’. The comparison ὡς εἰ … εἴη is ‘as if he were’, πάλαι ‘long since’, a Greek optative where English has a past.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐλεαίροντες δίδοσαν, καὶ ἐθάμβεον αὐτόν,
ἀλλήλους τ’ εἴροντο τίς εἴη καὶ πόθεν ἔλθοι.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ eleairontes didosan, kai ethambeon auton,
allēlous t’ eironto tis eiē kai pothen elthoi.
sentences.l:
And they, pitying, gave, and were amazed at him,
and one another they asked who he was and whence he had come.
sentences.i: And they gave out of pity, and were amazed at him, and asked one another who he was and where he had come from.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ ‘and they’ are the suitors, ἐλεαίροντες ‘pitying’ giving the reason for the gift. δίδοσαν is ‘they gave’, with no augment, and ἐθάμβεον is ‘they were amazed’. εἴροντο is the aorist middle of ἔρομαι ‘ask’. τίς εἴη and πόθεν ἔλθοι are indirect questions, with the optative after a past verb. The suitors are puzzled at his bearing, and the line prepares Melanthius’s speech.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe Melanthios, aipolos aigōn·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Melanthius, the goatherd of goats:
sentences.i: And Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, spoke up among them as well:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction. μετέειπε is ‘spoke among’ and τοῖσι ‘among them’ is the suitors. The name and epithet are the same as in 17.247: Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν, ‘goatherd of goats’, the same words being used for him again. καί is ‘also’.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης,
τοῦδε περὶ ξείνου·
sentences.tr:
keklyte meu, mnēstēres agakleitēs basileiēs,
toude peri xeinou·
sentences.l:
“Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen,
about this stranger;
sentences.i: “Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen, about this stranger;
sentences.n: Melanthius speaks. κέκλυτε is a perfect-form imperative of κλύω, ‘hear’, and μευ is the genitive ‘me’. βασιλείης is the genitive of a feminine noun ‘queen’, so that μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης are ‘suitors of the renowned queen’, Penelope; the dependent genitive says whose hand they seek. ἀγακλειτῆς is ‘renowned’. τοῦδε περὶ ξείνου is ‘about this stranger’, with περί standing between the demonstrative and its noun.

sentences.t: ἦ γάρ μιν πρόσθεν ὄπωπα.
sentences.tr: ē gar min prosthen opōpa.
sentences.l: for truly him before I have seen.
sentences.i: for I have seen him before.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. μιν is ‘him’, and πρόσθεν ‘before’. ὄπωπα is the perfect of ὁράω, ‘I have seen’. Melanthius met the beggar on the road in the part before, and that is the sighting he means.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι μέν οἱ δεῦρο συβώτης ἡγεμόνευεν,
αὐτὸν δ’ οὐ σάφα οἶδα, πόθεν γένος εὔχεται εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
ē toi men hoi deuro sybōtēs hēgemoneuen,
auton d’ ou sapha oida, pothen genos euchetai einai.
sentences.l:
Indeed the swineherd led him here,
but as for the man himself, I do not clearly know whence he claims to be by birth.”
sentences.i: The swineherd did bring him here, but as for the man himself, I do not clearly know where he claims to come from by birth.”
sentences.n: ἦ τοι μέν is ‘indeed’. οἱ is ‘for him, to him’, and ἡγεμόνευεν ‘was leading’. αὐτὸν δέ turns to ‘the man himself’, the object of οἶδα with οὐ σάφα ‘not clearly’. πόθεν is ‘whence’, and the clause πόθεν γένος εὔχεται εἶναι is ‘from where he claims to be in family’, γένος an accusative of respect; εὔχεται is ‘claims’ (εὔχομαι also means ‘pray’), and εἶναι is the infinitive.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἔπεσιν νείκεσσε συβώτην·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, Antinoos d’ epesin neikesse sybōtēn·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Antinous with words reviled the swineherd:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Antinous reviled the swineherd with words:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ὣς ἔφατο ‘so he spoke’. νείκεσσε is the aorist of νεικέω ‘revile, quarrel with’, with no augment, and ἔπεσιν ‘with words’ is a dative of means. The object is συβώτην. Antinous speaks to Eumaeus, not to Melanthius, who has said nothing against the beggar.

sentences.t:
ὦ ἀρίγνωτε συβῶτα, τίη δὲ σὺ τόνδε πόλινδε
ἤγαγες;
sentences.tr:
ō arignōte sybōta, tiē de sy tonde polinde
ēgages;
sentences.l:
“O easily-known swineherd, why then you this man to the city
led?
sentences.i: “You well-known swineherd, why have you brought this man to the city?
sentences.n: Antinous speaks, and the question runs over two lines. ἀρίγνωτε is the vocative of ἀρίγνωτος ‘easily known, well known’, perhaps meaning ‘notorious’; the tone is uncertain, and the word may be sarcastic. τίη is τί ‘why’, and δέ is ‘then’. τόνδε πόλινδε has the suffix -δε ‘to the city’. ἤγαγες is the aorist of ἄγω.

sentences.t:
ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ἧμιν ἀλήμονές εἰσι καὶ ἄλλοι,
πτωχοὶ ἀνιηροί, δαιτῶν ἀπολυμαντῆρες;
sentences.tr:
ē ouch halis hēmin alēmones eisi kai alloi,
ptōchoi aniēroi, daitōn apolymantēres;
sentences.l:
Or are there not enough for us, vagrants, even others,
beggars, irksome, spoilers of feasts?
sentences.i: Or are there not enough other vagrants among us already, irksome beggars, spoilers of feasts?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐχ opens a question that expects the answer ‘yes, there are enough’. ἧμιν is ‘for us’, an epic form of ἡμῖν. ἀλήμονες is ‘vagrants’, from ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, and καὶ ἄλλοι ‘others too’. πτωχοὶ ἀνιηροί is ‘irksome beggars’ (ἀνία ‘distress’), and δαιτῶν ἀπολυμαντῆρες ‘spoilers of feasts’, a rare word from λύμη ‘ruin’, whose sense is taken from that root.

sentences.t:
ἦ ὄνοσαι ὅτι τοι βίοτον κατέδουσιν ἄνακτος
ἐνθάδ’ ἀγειρόμενοι, σὺ δὲ καὶ προτὶ τόνδ’ ἐκάλεσσας;
sentences.tr:
ē onosai hoti toi bioton katedousin anaktos
enthad’ ageiromenoi, sy de kai proti tond’ ekalessas;
sentences.l:
Or do you make light of it that your lord’s livelihood they eat up,
gathering here, and you even in addition this man called in?”
sentences.i: Or do you make light of it that they eat up your lord’s livelihood, gathering here, and have you called in this man as well?”
sentences.n: ὄνοσαι is the second person of ὄνομαι ‘make light of, scorn, find fault with’, and ὅτι ‘that’ gives the matter taken lightly; the sense is taken from LSJ. τοι is σοι ‘your’, with ἄνακτος ‘lord’. βίοτον is ‘livelihood’, κατέδουσιν ‘eat up’. ἀγειρόμενοι is ‘gathering’, the beggars. προτί is πρός, an adverb ‘besides’, and ἐκάλεσσας ‘you called in’ is the aorist. Antinous speaks as though he were not himself eating Odysseus’s livelihood.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The same formula as 311: the poet addresses Eumaeus as ‘you’, προσέφης, and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα is ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’. This time the answer is to Antinous, and it is blunter than anything Eumaeus said to Odysseus.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνο’, οὐ μὲν καλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.tr: Antino’, ou men kala kai esthlos eōn agoreueis·
sentences.l: “Antinous, not indeed fair things, though a good man, do you say;
sentences.i: “Antinous, you do not speak well, good man though you are;
sentences.n: Eumaeus answers. Ἀντίνο’ is the vocative, with the last vowel elided. οὐ μὲν καλά is ‘not indeed fair things’, καλά being a neuter plural, the object of ἀγορεύεις, which English turns into ‘not well’. καὶ ἐσθλὸς ἐών is ‘though you are a good man’, καί giving the participle concessive force; ἐσθλός is ‘good’, and the phrase has an edge of reproach. ἀγορεύεις is ‘you speak’, and the line ends with an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τίς γὰρ δὴ ξεῖνον καλεῖ ἄλλοθεν αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν
ἄλλον γ’, εἰ μὴ τῶν οἳ δημιοεργοὶ ἔασι,
μάντιν ἢ ἰητῆρα κακῶν ἢ τέκτονα δούρων,
ἢ καὶ θέσπιν ἀοιδόν, ὅ κεν τέρπῃσιν ἀείδων;
sentences.tr:
tis gar dē xeinon kalei allothen autos epelthōn
allon g’, ei mē tōn hoi dēmioergoi easi,
mantin ē iētēra kakōn ē tektona dourōn,
ē kai thespin aoidon, ho ken terpēisin aeidōn;
sentences.l:
For who indeed a stranger invites, from elsewhere himself having come,
another, unless one of those who are craftsmen for the people,
a seer, or a healer of ills, or a carpenter of timbers,
or even an inspired minstrel, who may delight by singing?
sentences.i: For who goes himself from elsewhere and invites a stranger, another man, unless he is one of those who are craftsmen for the people: a seer, or a healer of ills, or a carpenter of timbers, or even an inspired minstrel, who may delight by his singing?
sentences.n: τίς … καλεῖ is ‘who invites’, a rhetorical question, with ἄλλοθεν ‘from elsewhere’ and αὐτὸς ἐπελθών ‘going himself’. ἄλλον γ’ is ‘another’, and εἰ μὴ τῶν οἳ is ‘unless one of those who’. δημιοεργοί is ‘craftsmen for the people’ (δῆμος and ἔργον), and ἔασι is εἰσί. τέκτονα δούρων is ‘carpenter of timbers’. θέσπιν is ‘inspired’. ὅ κεν τέρπῃσιν is ‘who may delight’, a relative with κεν and a subjunctive in -σιν.

sentences.t: οὗτοι γὰρ κλητοί γε βροτῶν ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr: houtoi gar klētoi ge brotōn ep’ apeirona gaian·
sentences.l: for these are the invited ones, among mortals, over the boundless earth;
sentences.i: for these are the men who are invited, among mortals, anywhere on the boundless earth;
sentences.n: οὗτοι γάρ is ‘for these’, the four trades just listed. κλητοί is ‘invited, called’, and γε stresses it. βροτῶν is ‘of mortals’, partitive: ‘among mortals’. ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is ‘over the boundless earth’, a phrase that closes this line and stands mid-line at 1.98, with ἀπείρων ‘boundless’. The stop after it is an ano teleia.

sentences.t: πτωχὸν δ’ οὐκ ἄν τις καλέοι τρύξοντα ἓ αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: ptōchon d’ ouk an tis kaleoi tryxonta he auton.
sentences.l: and a beggar not would anyone invite, to wear down himself.
sentences.i: but no one would invite a beggar who will wear down his host.
sentences.n: καλέοι is an optative with ἄν ‘would invite’, uncontracted. τρύξοντα is a future participle of τρύχω ‘wear down, exhaust’, agreeing with πτωχόν. ἓ αὐτόν is ‘himself’, ἕ being the reflexive of the third person, which refers back to the subject τις ‘anyone’: the host is the one who is worn down.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ χαλεπὸς περὶ πάντων εἶς μνηστήρων
δμωσὶν Ὀδυσσῆος, πέρι δ’ αὖτ’ ἐμοί·
sentences.tr:
all’ aiei chalepos peri pantōn eis mnēstērōn
dmōsin Odyssēos, peri d’ aut’ emoi·
sentences.l:
But always harsh above all you are of the suitors
to Odysseus’ servants, and above all, in turn, to me;
sentences.i: But of all the suitors you are always the harshest to the servants of Odysseus, and above all, in turn, to me;
sentences.n: The accent in εἶς shows that it is ‘you are’ (an old form of εἶ), the verb the sentence needs, and not the number ‘one’; χαλεπός is ‘harsh’, and περὶ πάντων … μνηστήρων is ‘beyond all the suitors’. δμωσίν is a dative, ‘to the servants’, in -σιν. πέρι is περί, ‘above all’, with the accent shifted, and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn, again’. The unit ends mid-line, at the ano teleia after ἐμοί, and αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε opens the next.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε
οὐκ ἀλέγω, ἧός μοι ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια
ζώει ἐνὶ μεγάροις καὶ Τηλέμαχος θεοειδής.
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge
ouk alegō, hēos moi echephrōn Pēnelopeia
zōei eni megarois kai Tēlemachos theoeidēs.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part,
do not care, so long as for me sound-minded Penelope
lives in the halls, and Telemachus, godlike in form.”
sentences.i: but I do not care, so long as sound-minded Penelope lives in the halls, and Telemachus, godlike in form.”
sentences.n: The cut falls mid-line. ἐγώ γε is ‘I for my part’. ἀλέγω is ‘I care, I heed’, and ἧος is ‘as long as’. μοι is ‘for me’. ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια is ‘sound-minded Penelope’, ἐχέφρων taking its meaning from ἔχω and φρήν; ζώει is ‘lives’, uncontracted from ζώω. Τηλέμαχος θεοειδής is ‘Telemachus, godlike in form’, his standing epithet.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply: αὖ ‘in turn’, πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’, and ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’, with ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω, augmented (αὐ- lengthened to ηὐ-). τόν is ‘him’, Eumaeus, who has just spoken.

sentences.t: σίγα, μή μοι τοῦτον ἀμείβεο πολλὰ ἔπεσσιν·
sentences.tr: siga, mē moi touton ameibeo polla epessin·
sentences.l: “Be silent, do not for me this man answer much with words;
sentences.i: “Be silent, and do not answer this man at length with words, I ask you;
sentences.n: Telemachus speaks to Eumaeus. σίγα is ‘be silent’, an imperative from σιγάω, and μή with the imperative ἀμείβεο (ἀμείβου, an uncontracted second person middle) is a prohibition. μοι is ‘for me’, a dative of interest. τοῦτον is ‘this man’, Antinous, the object of ἀμείβεο ‘answer’. πολλά is ‘at length’, an accusative of extent, and ἔπεσσιν is ‘with words’, a dative in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνοος δ’ εἴωθε κακῶς ἐρεθιζέμεν αἰεὶ
μύθοισιν χαλεποῖσιν, ἐποτρύνει δὲ καὶ ἄλλους.
sentences.tr:
Antinoos d’ eiōthe kakōs erethizemen aiei
mythoisin chalepoisin, epotrynei de kai allous.
sentences.l:
for Antinous is accustomed ill to provoke always
with harsh words, and he urges on others also.”
sentences.i: for Antinous is always in the habit of provoking people spitefully with harsh words, and he urges others on as well.”
sentences.n: εἴωθε is a perfect, ‘is accustomed’, with the infinitive ἐρεθιζέμεν ‘to provoke’, a form in -έμεν (Attic -έναι). κακῶς is ‘ill, spitefully’. μύθοισιν χαλεποῖσιν is ‘with harsh words’, a dative in -οισιν. ἐποτρύνει is ‘urges on’, with καὶ ἄλλους ‘others too’: Antinous is blamed for the bad temper of the rest as well.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ Ἀντίνοον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai Antinoon epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: He spoke, and to Antinous too winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he said, and turned to speak winged words to Antinous:
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is ‘so he spoke, and’, a narrative use of ἦ ῥα (compare 356). Ἀντίνοον is the object of προσηύδα ‘spoke to’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the formula ‘winged words’, and προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω, ‘spoke to’, with its augment inside the compound (προσ-ηύδα). Telemachus now turns from Eumaeus to Antinous.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, ἦ μευ καλὰ πατὴρ ὣς κήδεαι υἷος,
ὃς τὸν ξεῖνον ἄνωγας ἀπὸ μεγάροιο διέσθαι
μύθῳ ἀναγκαίῳ·
sentences.tr:
Antino’, ē meu kala patēr hōs kēdeai huios,
hos ton xeinon anōgas apo megaroio diesthai
mythōi anankaiōi·
sentences.i: “Antinous, what fine care you take of me, as a father does for his son: you who give orders to drive this stranger away from the hall with a compelling word;
sentences.n: Antinous is the vocative, elided. The line is ironic. κήδεαι is ‘you care’ (κήδομαι, with the genitive μευ ‘for me’), and πατὴρ ὣς … υἷος is ‘as a father for a son’, with κήδεται understood. ὃς … ἄνωγας ‘you who bid’ takes an infinitive διέσθαι ‘to drive away’, from δίεμαι ‘drive, chase’; the Greek does not say who is to do the driving. μύθῳ ἀναγκαίῳ is ‘with a word of compulsion’, an order that cannot be resisted.

sentences.t: μὴ τοῦτο θεὸς τελέσειε.
sentences.tr: mē touto theos teleseie.
sentences.l: may a god not bring this to pass.
sentences.i: may a god not bring this to pass.
sentences.n: μή with an optative is a wish against: τελέσειε is ‘may he bring to pass’, an aorist optative of τελέω, so ‘may a god not accomplish this’. The sense runs back to διέσθαι: let no god make true the order to drive the stranger off. θεός is not named, and the wish asks nothing of any one god.

sentences.t: δός οἱ ἑλών· οὔ τοι φθονέω· κέλομαι γὰρ ἐγώ γε·
sentences.tr: dos hoi helōn· ou toi phthoneō· kelomai gar egō ge·
sentences.l: Give to him, having taken it; I do not grudge it to you; for I bid it, I myself;
sentences.i: Take something and give it to him: I do not begrudge it to you, for I myself bid you.
sentences.n: Three short sentences share one line, each ended by an ano teleia. δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and οἱ is ‘to him’. ἑλών is ‘having taken’, the aorist participle of αἱρέω, which does the work of ‘take something’. τοι may be σοι ‘to you’ or the particle ‘indeed’, and the sense is the same. φθονέω is ‘I begrudge’, κέλομαι ‘I bid’, and ἐγώ γε ‘I at least’.

sentences.t:
μήτ’ οὖν μητέρ’ ἐμὴν ἅζευ τό γε μήτε τιν’ ἄλλον
δμώων, οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.tr:
mēt’ oun mēter’ emēn hazeu to ge mēte tin’ allon
dmōōn, hoi kata dōmat’ Odyssēos theioio.
sentences.l:
nor then my mother shrink from, in this at least, nor any other
of the servants who are throughout the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: So do not shrink from my mother in this, nor from any other of the servants in the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἅζευ is the imperative of ἅζομαι ‘stand in awe of, shrink from’, with μητέρα ἐμήν and τιν’ ἄλλον as its objects. μήτε … μήτε is ‘neither … nor’, οὖν ‘then’, and τό γε ‘in this at least’ is an accusative of respect. δμώων is ‘of the servants’ (partitive); οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ means ‘who are in the house’, with εἰσί understood, and θείοιο is ‘divine’, an epithet of Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ τοι τοιοῦτον ἐνὶ στήθεσσι νόημα·
αὐτὸς γὰρ φαγέμεν πολὺ βούλεαι ἢ δόμεν ἄλλῳ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou toi toiouton eni stēthessi noēma·
autos gar phagemen poly bouleai ē domen allōi.
sentences.l:
But not indeed such a thought is in your breast;
for yourself to eat much rather you wish than to give to another.”
sentences.i: But you have no such thought in your breast: you would much rather eat yourself than give to another.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὔ τοι is ‘but not indeed’, and the line has no verb: ‘there is not such a thought’. νόημα is ‘thought, purpose’, and στήθεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, ‘breast’. αὐτός ‘you yourself’ is stressed. φαγέμεν is ‘to eat’, an aorist infinitive in -έμεν, and δόμεν ‘to give’ (Attic δοῦναι). βούλεαι is ‘you wish’ (βούλῃ), and πολύ with ἤ gives ‘much rather … than’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Antinoos apameibomenos proseeipe·
sentences.l: Him then in turn, answering, addressed Antinous:
sentences.i: In answer Antinous said to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula that joins two others: αὖτ’ is ‘in turn’, as in τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε, and ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, as in τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη. προσέειπε is ‘addressed’, and τόν is ‘him’, Telemachus. No new paragraph begins here, and the speaker simply changes.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχ’ ὑψαγόρη, μένος ἄσχετε, ποῖον ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: Tēlemach’ hypsagorē, menos aschete, poion eeipes.
sentences.l: “Telemachus, lofty-talker, unrestrained-in-fury, what a thing you have said!
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you lofty talker, unrestrained in your fury, what a thing you have said!
sentences.n: Antinous speaks. Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative, elided. ὑψαγόρη ‘lofty-talker’ and μένος ἄσχετε ‘unrestrained in fury’ are two vocative insults, the same pair of insults as at 2.85 and 2.303. ποῖον is exclamatory, ‘what a thing’, and ἔειπες is an aorist, ‘you said’.

sentences.t:
εἴ οἱ τόσσον ἅπαντες ὀρέξειαν μνηστῆρες,
καί κέν μιν τρεῖς μῆνας ἀπόπροθεν οἶκος ἐρύκοι.
sentences.tr:
ei hoi tosson hapantes orexeian mnēstēres,
kai ken min treis mēnas apoprothen oikos erykoi.
sentences.l:
If to him so much all were to hold out, the suitors,
then even three months far off the house would keep him away.
sentences.i: If all the suitors were to hold out so much to him, the house would keep him off at a distance for three months.
sentences.n: A condition with the optative: εἰ … ὀρέξειαν is ‘if they were to hold out’ (ὀρέγω ‘reach out, hand over’), with οἱ ‘to him’ and τόσσον ‘so much’, answered by καί κεν … ἐρύκοι ‘would keep off’. τρεῖς μῆνας is ‘three months’, the length of time. ἀπόπροθεν is ‘far away’. Antinous’s speech runs on into the next part, so it has no closing mark here. οἶκος is ‘house’, and the Greek does not say whose.
